title: This Octopus Can Learn Who You Are

scenes.notes: A giant Pacific octopus can learn who you are.
Not people in general. You, and whether you fed it or poked it.
It's the largest octopus species, and spread wide, its arms reach past twice your height.

scenes.notes: There's no bone in it. Only a parrot-like beak, so any gap wider than that beak is a door.
Its arms carry over two thousand suckers, and each one can taste what it grabs. Including you.

scenes.notes: In under a second its skin matches the rock behind you. Its saliva carries a venom that leaves a crab limp.

scenes.notes: But that's still not the strangest part. Most of its nerve cells sit in its arms, so each arm can explore alone.
Back to you. In two thousand ten, at the Seattle Aquarium, two people dressed alike visited eight of these octopuses.
One always brought food. The other prodded them with a bristly stick. Within two weeks, the octopuses treated them differently.
So say you're the stick person. Disguise? Matching clothes didn't fool them. Locked tank? Remember the door. The dark? Its arms taste you.
Here's the twist. It doesn't want a fight. Bites on people are rare; it would rather vanish behind a cloud of ink.
And it hasn't long to hold a grudge. It lives three to five years, and a mother stops eating to guard her eggs, then dies as they hatch.
So be the one with the food. For the few years it gets, it knows who you are.
